newsitem.title: JORDAN: Jordan court told soldier might be mentally ill.
newsitem.headline: Jordan court told soldier might be mentally ill.

text.p: Independant medical psychologists told a military court on Sunday that a Jordanian soldier charged with killing seven Israeli schoolgirls might be mentally ill.

Two psychologists brought by the defence to testify also questioned the medical soundness of evidence by military psychologists who concluded Private Ahmed Daqamsa was not mentally ill but had "an anti-social personality disorder".

"The anti-social personality disorder is a form of mental illness," said psychologist Ahmed Ali Khalafh, who said its sufferers might react voilently in an "explosive" way at the slightest provocation and not be aware of their own actions.

Daqamsa has said he was praying at Baqoura on the day of the shooting last March, when the Israeli girls started mimicking him and laughing at him. He said he went to his car and picked up his rifle but could not recall what happened next.
Jordanian and Israeli witnesses said he fired off around 70 bullets from his automatic rifle at the group of Israelis, killing seven of them, aged 11 to 13.
Another defence witness, psychologist, Mohammed Kannan, also said victims of anti-social personality disorder could not be held responsible for their actions.

Both Khalaf and Kanaan said after questioning by the defence military psychologists who filmed Daqamsa on video without his knowledge or approval during medical diagnosis of his case were in breach of medical ethics. The prosecution said they plan to use the tapes as part of the evidence against the soldier.
Military prosecutors charged that Daqamsa plotted to kill Israelis for months ahead of the shooting and volunteered extra guard duties so he would have the chance to strike.

The defence are trying to prove he acted impulsively and are using evidence of a history of mental disturbance which emerged in the course of the trial to show the soldier bore no responsiblity for his actions and acted on the spur of the moment.
Daqamsa was stationed in Jordan's northern border territory of Baqoura, formally returned by Israel under a 1994 peace treaty but leased back to Israeli farmers.
The shooting of the Israelis and Daqamsa's subsequent trial has highlighted the deep divisions in Jordan over the accord.
King Hussein said Daqamsa had shamed Jordan's army and said he should have been shot dead on the spot. But opponents of the peace treaty with Israel have rallied to defend him.
